# Answer key — Chapter 07: Hardening and access control {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-07-identity-perimeter · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The section opens with exactly this consolidation: one web console and one
API, both Internet-reachable, so a stolen administrator credential can be
control of everything at once; a is false (firewalls still exist, Session 4),
c confuses IAM with TLS, and d misstates shared responsibility.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-07-authentication-mfa · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
@def-mfa requires evidence from more than one independent category;
a password and a hardware token combine *knows* and *has*, while a, c and d
each combine two examples of a single category (knows/knows, knows/knows,
is/is).

**Q3** *(tests @sec-07-identity-perimeter · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"an entitlement maps identities to authorisations, often with conditions
(identity X may access resource Y when attributes Z hold)"; "the entitlement
matrix is the table of these mappings, written down and reviewed to show
whether least privilege holds" (any phrasing that names the identity→
authorisation mapping and the written table used for review).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-07-authorisation-models · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The Guidance names PBAC supporting ABAC as the preferred model and
recommends ABAC and PBAC over RBAC where the platform supports them
(CSA, 2024, pp. 115, 122); RBAC's simplicity (a) is real but is not the
Guidance's preference, and c and d mix in unrelated concepts.

**Q5** *(tests @sec-07-protection-domains · basic)* — **Accepted answers:**
"a protection domain is a set of (object, rights) pairs: which operations one
actor may perform on which objects"; "on UNIX/Linux a process's protection
domain is defined by its user and group identifiers (UID and GID)" (any
phrasing naming (object, rights) pairs and UID/GID).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-07-sso-pam · basic)* — **Correct: b.**
The chapter states there is no single master password (which rules out a);
each staff member holds administrative rights only on their own systems, and
the PAM system logs accesses and alerts on suspicious privileged use — PAM
is least privilege applied to administrators, not a replacement for MFA (c)
or a firewall rule (d).

**Q7** *(tests @sec-07-credentials-management-plane · basic)* — **Accepted
answers:** "elevated access requested for a session, approved, and revoked
when the session ends"; "it addresses static credentials — long-lived
secrets such as API keys — because no permanent key exists to steal" (any
phrasing with request/approve/revoke per session and the static-credential
hazard).

**Q8 — applied scenario** *(tests @sec-07-exercises · applied)* —
**Model answer:** What it fixes: the password is no longer casually shared or
reused, and reaching it now requires MFA — the password manager raises the
cost of theft. What it still gets wrong: (1) the Nextcloud account itself
still accepts a password alone, so a phished or breached password still logs
in — MFA must be on the administrator account (@def-mfa), not only in front
of the vault; (2) it is still one shared login, so no action can be traced to
a person, which undermines the logs of Session 10 and the monitoring of
Session 9; (3) least privilege (@def-leastpriv) is untouched — everyone with
vault access holds full administrative power whether their task needs it or
not. Change: per-person accounts with MFA on each, administrative rights only
for those who need them (ordinary members get member access), ideally granted
just in time. **Grading notes:** full credit requires naming both remaining
failures (no MFA on the account itself / no traceability) plus least
privilege; partial credit for recognising only one of them; the concrete
change proposed must include per-person accounts with MFA.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-07-authn-vs-authz — Authentication vs authorisation)*
Authentication verifies identity; authorisation decides permitted
actions. A system authenticates a user correctly but then grants them
administrator rights they do not need: correct identity, excessive
authorisation.

(2) *(@exr-07-three-factors — The three authentication factors)*
Something one knows (password/PIN), something one has
(phone/hardware token), something one is (biometric); MFA requires more than
one category, so a stolen password satisfies only one factor and fails alone.

(3) *(@exr-07-cloud-needs-mfa — Why the cloud needs MFA)*
Broad network access: cloud services are reached over the Internet, so a
lost or stolen credential leads to account takeover without the attacker
being anywhere near the victim, and passwords alone cannot carry that risk.

(4) *(@exr-07-rbac-vs-abac — RBAC vs ABAC)*
RBAC grants permissions to roles and assigns identities to roles, simple
but coarse; ABAC decides from attributes and context, fine-grained and
context-aware. The Guidance prefers ABAC (and PBAC) where supported; both
serve least privilege by granting only what the task and context require.

(5) *(@exr-07-shared-admin — Shared admin account as threat–risk–control)*
Threat: the shared password is phished or reused, giving an attacker full
control of all files. Risk: high likelihood, maximal impact (all three CIA
properties). Controls: require MFA on the admin account, apply least privilege
to members, and replace the shared login with per-person accounts so that
each action can be traced to a person.
